arguments.content:
*clears throat, settles onto the big rock at the front of the pond*

Alright, alright, quit shoving each other. Everybody get your tails settled. Who threw that snail? Don't look at me like that, Boggins, I saw you.

Right. Story time.

This one's called **The Iron Heron and the Toads Who Had No General.**

---

Long time ago — before your mothers were eggs, before MY mother was an egg — there was a stretch of wetland called the Fenns. Huge place. Miles of bog and black water and reed forests thick enough to get lost in for days. And in the Fenns lived about ten thousand toads, spread across maybe forty different pools.

Now here's the thing about the Fenns toads. They didn't have a chief. They didn't have a council of elders who sat around making rules for everyone. Nobody wore a crown. Nobody collected taxes in flies.

What they had was each other.

If a pool dried up in summer, the toads from that pool would just... walk to the next one. And the toads already there would shift over, dig the banks wider, make room. Nobody asked permission. Nobody had to. You see a toad carrying her eggs through cracked mud, you don't check with management. You just help her dig.

If someone was good at something — say, Old Muckjaw knew every safe crossing through heron territory, or Pebbletongue could smell a snake den from two hundred hops away — other toads would come to them for that thing. Not because those toads had titles. Because they'd earned trust by being right, over and over, and being willing to share what they knew. And the moment Muckjaw got sloppy or Pebbletongue started making things up, toads would stop listening. Simple as that. Trust given freely, taken back just as free.

They settled fights by talking. Sometimes loudly. Sometimes two toads would just croak at each other for an hour in the shallows until one of them laughed or both of them got hungry. But nobody got to lock anybody up. Nobody got banished because one powerful toad said so. If you wronged someone, you faced them, and you faced the toads who cared about them, and you worked it out or you lived with the shame. That was enough. It almost always was.

So. That's how things were. Forty pools, ten thousand toads, no boss. And it worked. For generations it worked.

Then the Iron Heron came.

---

Now stop squirming, this is the good part.

Upstream from the Fenns there was a beaver kingdom. Good creatures, the beavers. Organized different from the toads — they had their Lodge Chief and their ranked builders and all of that. It worked fine for them. Beavers like structure. They build dams, and dams need blueprints, and blueprints need someone saying "this log goes HERE not THERE." Fair enough.

But their latest Lodge Chief, a massive old beaver named Ironpelt, he'd been having trouble with a heron. Not a normal heron. This thing was a machine.

Some creature — nobody ever found out who — had built it. A heron made of black iron and copper wire, tall as three beavers stacked, with glass eyes that glowed orange at dusk. It moved on legs that hissed with steam. It had a beak that could punch through a beaver dam like it was wet leaves. And it was hungry. Not for fish. For territory. It smashed dams. It flooded lodges. It drove the beavers south.

Ironpelt sent scouts to the Fenns. Two beavers, polite enough, showed up at the biggest toad pool and asked to speak to "whoever's in charge."

The toads just looked at each other.

"In charge of what?" said a toad named Dreg, who happened to be closest.

The beavers explained. The Iron Heron was coming south. It would hit the Fenns within a moon. They needed to coordinate a defense. They needed a general, a war leader, someone who could command the toad forces.

Dreg scratched her chin. "We don't do that," she said.

The beavers were confused. "You don't do defense?"

"We don't do generals."

The beavers left worried. Honestly? The toads were worried too. A machine that kills — that's not something you handle by croaking loudly in the shallows.

That night, Dreg hopped to the next pool over and told them what she'd heard. Those toads told the next pool. By sunrise, the news had moved across all forty pools, no messenger system, no chain of command. Just toads talking to toads.

And then something happened that the beavers never would have predicted.

Nobody gave an order. But everybody started working.

---

A toad named Sumpwhistle — nasty old creature, missing one eye, you'd hate her at first but she'd die for you — she'd spent years studying the creek mechanics of the Fenns. Where the water pooled. Where it ran fast. She'd never been elected to anything. She just knew water. She started drawing maps in the mud, showing where you could flood a channel fast, where you could drain one. Other toads gathered around, not because she told them to, but because her maps made sense.

A young toad called Rivet — barely older than you lot — had been picking apart old human trash at the edge of the wetland. Broken machines, rusted wire, cracked gears. Junk to most. But Rivet understood how the pieces fit. She started sketching something. A device. A vast thing.

"If the Iron Heron runs on steam," Rivet said, "then it needs heat. It needs dry. What does it NOT need?"

"Mud," said someone.

"Mud," said Rivet. "And what do we have more of than any creature alive?"

She designed a machine of her own. Not iron — she used reed bundles and creek clay and sinew and rocks. A series of channels and release gates that could, with the pull of a few vines, flood an entire valley floor with deep, thick, sucking mud. She called it the Gulper.

Now here's what's important: Rivet didn't just announce "I'm building the Gulper, everyone help me." She explained what she wanted to do. Other toads poked holes in the plan. A toad named Brank said the western channel wouldn't hold and he was right, so they redesigned it. A pool of toads near the southern reed forest said they wouldn't join, not out of cowardice but because they had sick tadpoles to guard, and nobody shamed them for it. Thirty or so toads from the eastern pools said they had a different idea — they wanted to rig noise traps, banks of hollow reeds that would scream when the wind blew through them, to disorient the machine. Great, said the others. Do it.

No one coordinated from the top. Toads just found the gap that fit their shape, and filled it.

The beavers sent another scout. She watched the toads working and was baffled. "Who is running this?" she asked.

Five different toads pointed at five different things and said, "I'm handling this part."

The beaver asked, "But what if one part fails?"

Old Sumpwhistle croaked from her mud map: "Then the other parts keep going. We don't stack everything on one back. If I get eaten tomorrow, these maps are drawn in mud that twenty toads already memorized."

---

The Iron Heron came on a Tuesday.

It came through the northern pass, steam curling from its joints, those glass eyes scanning. Huge. Terrible. Beautiful, in a way, if you could forget it was here to wreck your home.

The noise traps hit first. The eastern reeds screamed like a thousand frogs in a thunderstorm. The machine stuttered. Its head swiveled, confused. It wasn't built to handle sounds coming from everywhere and nowhere.

While it was turning, Sumpwhistle's drainage team opened the first gate. Water surged across the northern flats, and the ground turned to soup. The Iron Heron's legs sank to the knee joints. Steam hissed from the seams as water crept into its workings.

It pulled free. It adapted. That beak came down like a hammer and smashed one of the flood gates to splinters. Six toads scrambled clear. One didn't make it — a digger named Fallow, crushed under the debris. First death. The toads didn't stop working, but they felt it. You always feel it.

The Heron pushed south. That's when Rivet pulled the Gulper.

Four vines, pulled by four teams who couldn't even see each other through the reeds. But they'd rehearsed. They'd talked it through. They knew the timing because they'd practiced together, voluntarily, not because a drill sergeant made them.

The Gulper opened. An entire hillside reservoir dropped its load. A river of cold, thick swamp mud rolled through the central Fenns like a slow brown avalanche. It caught the Iron Heron mid-stride. The machine sank. Mud in the gears. Mud in the steam vents. Mud in those glass eyes. It thrashed. It swung that beak blind and screaming.

And a hundred toads, from a dozen different pools, none of them ordered to be there, closed in with ropes of braided vine and pulled it down.

It took hours. It was ugly. The Iron Heron broke Brank's leg with one last kick. But by dawn, it was just a shape in the mud, half-buried, steam dead, eyes dark.

---

After it was over, the beavers came down to see. Ironpelt himself, the Lodge Chief. He stood at the edge of the mud field and stared at what the toads had done.

"Who do I thank?" he asked.

Dreg was there. Muddy to her eyeballs. She shrugged.

"Thank the Fenns," she said. "It was all of us. Or don't thank anybody. We didn't do it for thanks. We did it because this is where we live."

Ironpelt respected that. The beavers helped dig out the wreckage and used the iron to reinforce their own dams further north. Good trade. The toads didn't want the scrap metal anyway.

Fallow's pool built a stone marker where she fell. Toads still visit it.

Rivet went back to picking through junk at the wetland's edge. She didn't want fame. She wanted to see how things worked.

Sumpwhistle complained about her knees for the rest of her life, which was long.

Nobody became a general after. Nobody said "that worked so well, let's pick a permanent leader." Because the whole point — the reason it worked — was that it DIDN'T depend on one toad. It depended on all of them choosing to show up.

---

*leans forward on the rock*

That's how it was. That's how it is. That's how it's going to be, long as you lot remember it.

We don't need someone sitting on a high rock telling us what to do. We need each other. We need to listen to the toad who knows the water and the toad who knows the wires and the toad who knows when to shut up and dig.

The beavers have their way. It builds good dams. The fish have their schools with their lead swimmers. It keeps them alive. Every creature finds the shape that fits.

Ours is this: nobody rules. Everybody matters. You help because it's right, not because someone made you. And when the iron things come — and they always come, sooner or later — you face them together, not because a general said to, but because the toad beside you is your neighbor, and the mud beneath you is your home.

Now go catch some flies. You've earned it.

And Boggins — put that snail back.
